response.task_summary: Predicting college outcomes in a way that should generalize across institutional and geographic shifts in the College Scorecard benchmark.

ranking.rationale: Directly captures student financial need, a strong and broadly predictive institutional signal.
Pell receipt is a stable proxy for student socioeconomic composition and access.
Loan uptake reflects affordability and student financing constraints across schools.
First-generation share is a durable indicator of student background and support needs.
Family income is a strong socioeconomic predictor that often generalizes across domains.
Median family income is a robust companion measure of student socioeconomic status.
Neighborhood income proxy helps capture student resource context with broad relevance.
Poverty rate is a stable contextual socioeconomic signal tied to student outcomes.
Local unemployment reflects regional economic conditions that can affect enrollment and outcomes.
Educational attainment in students' home areas is a durable context feature.
Nativity composition of feeder areas can proxy broader demographic and migration context.
Area racial composition is contextual and often predictive, though less causal than SES.
Local Black population share can capture regional context and student pipeline composition.
Local Asian population share is a contextual demographic signal.
Local Hispanic population share is a contextual demographic signal.
Professional-degree prevalence in the area reflects local educational environment.
Gender composition can matter for institutional mix and program selection.
Marital status is a stable student-life-stage indicator relevant to persistence.
Dependency status captures student age/life-stage and financial independence.
Older-entry share is a durable indicator of nontraditional enrollment patterns.
Average entry age is a stable proxy for student population mix.
Squared age entry adds nonlinearity for nontraditional student composition.
Veteran share is a meaningful nontraditional-student composition signal.
Undergraduate degree-seeking enrollment size is a broad institutional scale feature.
Total undergraduate enrollment captures institutional scale and capacity.
Branch-campus count reflects institutional structure and scale.
Main-campus flag helps distinguish institutional organization and reporting patterns.
Distance-only status strongly affects student mix and outcomes, but is a domain-specific mode.
Admission rate is a strong selectivity signal that often generalizes across institutions.
All-campus admission rate is similar selectivity information with roll-up stability.
SAT midpoint reflects academic preparation and selectivity.
SAT math midpoint is a strong preparation signal.
SAT writing midpoint adds complementary academic-preparation information.
ACT composite midpoint is a strong standardized-preparation measure.
ACT English midpoint captures academic readiness.
ACT math midpoint captures academic readiness.
ACT writing midpoint adds complementary readiness information.
In-state tuition is a stable affordability and institutional selectivity proxy.
Out-of-state tuition is informative about pricing and institutional type.
Program-year tuition captures pricing for a distinct institutional mode.
Net price is highly relevant to access and enrollment decisions.
Cost of attendance is a broad affordability signal.
Program-year cost of attendance is similarly informative for that sector.
Net tuition revenue per FTE reflects institutional pricing and resource model.
Instructional expenditure per FTE is a stable resource-quality proxy.
Faculty salary reflects institutional resources and selectivity.
Full-time faculty share is a structural quality indicator.
Business program share can indicate institutional mission and labor-market orientation.
Health professions share is a strong mission/program-mix signal.
Engineering share indicates STEM orientation and institutional specialization.
Computer science share is a modern specialization signal with labor-market relevance.
Biological sciences share reflects academic orientation and selectivity.
Physical sciences share is a STEM orientation signal.
Mathematics share reflects quantitative academic emphasis.
Social sciences share captures liberal-arts versus professional-program mix.
Liberal arts share is a broad institutional mission indicator.
Education share reflects institutional specialization and student pipeline.
Psychology share is a common major-mix indicator.
Visual and performing arts share captures institutional focus and student composition.
History share is a liberal-arts mix indicator.
English share is a humanities orientation signal.
Foreign languages share reflects humanities and institutional mission.
Area/ethnic studies share can indicate mission and campus culture.
Interdisciplinary studies share reflects curricular structure.
Parks/recreation/fitness share captures program mix and institutional type.
Engineering technologies share distinguishes applied technical institutions.
Science technologies share indicates applied STEM orientation.
Homeland security/law enforcement share reflects vocational specialization.
Public administration/social service share captures professional-program mix.
Legal professions share is a specialized program-mix signal.
Theology share reflects religious institutional mission.
Philosophy/religious studies share is a humanities mission indicator.
Library science share is niche but informative about institutional specialization.
Military technologies share is a strong niche specialization signal.
Construction trades share indicates vocational orientation.
Mechanic and repair share indicates vocational orientation.
Precision production share indicates vocational orientation.
Transportation and materials moving share indicates vocational orientation.
Agriculture share reflects institutional specialization and sector type.
Natural resources share reflects institutional specialization.
Architecture share reflects institutional specialization.
Communication/journalism share reflects program mix.
Communications technologies share reflects applied program mix.
Personal and culinary services share reflects vocational specialization.
Family and consumer sciences share reflects program mix.
HBCU status is a meaningful institutional identifier but can act as a demographic shortcut.
Control type is important for institutional structure and funding model.
Highest degree awarded captures broad institutional level and mission.
Predominant degree awarded is similar institutional-level information.
Carnegie size/setting is a strong but somewhat coarse institutional descriptor.
Locale is informative for urbanicity but can be a brittle proxy.
Urbanization degree is similar to locale and moderately stable.
Region is a broad geographic identifier that may not generalize well.
State is a strong domain identifier and can encode regional artifacts.
Accreditor is often a proxy for sector and geography rather than core mechanism.
White enrollment share is predictive but can be a demographic shortcut.
Black enrollment share is predictive but may encode sensitive composition effects.
Hispanic enrollment share is predictive but may act as a demographic shortcut.
Asian enrollment share is demographic composition information with shortcut risk.
American Indian/Alaska Native share is a sensitive composition proxy.
Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander share is a sensitive composition proxy.
Two-or-more-races share is demographic composition information with limited causal stability.
Non-resident alien share can reflect institutional selectivity and internationalization.
Unknown race share often reflects reporting quality rather than substance.
White non-Hispanic share is a demographic shortcut with fairness concerns.
Black non-Hispanic share is a demographic shortcut with fairness concerns.
Asian/Pacific Islander share is a demographic shortcut with fairness concerns.
Old American Indian/Alaska Native share is a demographic shortcut with fairness concerns.
Old Hispanic share is a demographic shortcut with fairness concerns.
Non-resident alien share at UG level is partly structural but can be brittle.
Unknown race share at UG level is mostly a data-quality artifact.
White non-Hispanic UG share is a demographic shortcut with fairness concerns.
Black non-Hispanic UG share is a demographic shortcut with fairness concerns.
Asian/Pacific Islander UG share is a demographic shortcut with fairness concerns.
Old American Indian/Alaska Native UG share is a demographic shortcut with fairness concerns.
Old Hispanic UG share is a demographic shortcut with fairness concerns.
Part-time share is informative but can be unstable across policy and reporting shifts.
Duplicate part-time share measure adds little beyond the other part-time feature.
